content: In physics, a free surface is defined as the surface of a body that is not subjected to perpendicular (normal) stress or parallel shear stress. An example of this is the boundary between two homogeneous fluids, such as liquid water and the air in Earth's atmosphere. Unlike liquids, gases cannot independently form a free surface. A liquid in a gravitational field will form a free surface if it is not confined from above. When in mechanical equilibrium, this free surface must be perpendicular to the forces acting on the liquid. If it were not, a force would exist along the surface, causing the liquid to flow in that direction. Consequently, on Earth's surface, all free surfaces of liquids are horizontal unless disturbed. Exceptions occur near solids dipping into the liquid, where surface tension locally distorts the surface. In a free liquid at rest, meaning one influenced only by internal attractive forces and not by external forces such as gravity, the free surface will naturally assume the shape with the least surface area for its volume—a perfect sphere. This phenomenon can be observed experimentally by placing a large globule of oil beneath the surface of a water-alcohol mixture with the same density, rendering the oil neutrally buoyant. If the free surface of a liquid is disturbed, waves are generated on the surface. These waves are not elastic waves caused by elastic forces but are instead gravity waves. Gravity acts to restore the disturbed liquid surface to its horizontal level, but due to momentum, the surface overshoots, leading to oscillations and the propagation of the disturbance to neighboring areas of the surface. The velocity of these surface waves depends on the square root of their wavelength when the liquid is deep, meaning longer waves on the sea travel faster than shorter ones. Very small waves, or ripples, are not caused by gravity but by capillary action. These ripples have properties distinct from longer ocean surface waves because the ripples increase the surface area, and capillary forces become significant compared to gravitational forces. When a liquid is contained in a cylindrical vessel and rotates around a vertical axis coinciding with the cylinder's axis, the free surface assumes a parabolic shape of revolution, known as a paraboloid. At each point on the free surface, the surface is perpendicular to the resultant force acting on it. This resultant force is a combination of gravitational force and the centrifugal force generated by the circular motion of each point. If a free liquid rotates about an axis, its free surface takes the shape of an oblate spheroid, which is the approximate shape of Earth due to its equatorial bulge. In hydrodynamics, the free surface is mathematically defined by the free-surface condition. In fluid dynamics, a free-surface vortex, also called a potential vortex or whirlpool, forms in irrotational flow, such as when a bathtub is drained. In naval architecture and marine safety, the free surface effect occurs when liquids or granular materials under a free surface in partially filled tanks or holds shift as the vessel heels. In hydraulic engineering, a free-surface jet is one where the entrainment of fluid outside the jet is minimal, unlike a submerged jet where entrainment effects are significant. A liquid jet in air approximates a free-surface jet. In fluid mechanics, a free-surface flow, also known as open channel flow, refers to the gravity-driven flow of a fluid under a free surface, such as water flowing under air in the atmosphere.
